title: Rate Limit Headers
description: Use standard and draft rate limit headers to communicate quota, remaining requests, and reset time to API clients.

data.text: Rate limit headers let clients know their current quota without guessing. Without them, clients hit 429 errors randomly and have no way to self-regulate. With them, clients can pace their requests intelligently.

data.title: Response headers for a healthy and limited request
data.content: Every response should include rate limit headers so clients can track their usage.
data.code:
# Request allowed (42 of 100 remaining)
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1728203460

{
  "id": "prod_881",
  "name": "Wireless Headphones"
}

# Request rejected (0 remaining, retry in 6s)
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1728203460
Retry-After: 6

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/rate-limited",
  "title": "Rate Limited",
  "status": 429,
  "retryAfter": 6
  }
}

data.text: The IETF draft (now RFC 6585 Section 8) defines RateLimit-* headers. While not universally adopted yet, they are becoming the standard. Support both old and new header names for maximum compatibility.

items: RateLimit-Reset — can be seconds or unix timestamp; document which you use
Set both header sets during a transition period
Prefer the RFC 6585 headers in new APIs

data.text: Well-behaved clients use rate limit headers to pace themselves. They do not wait for a 429 before slowing down.

items: When remaining drops below a threshold (e.g., 10), start backing off
On 429, read Retry-After and wait exactly that long before retrying
Implement exponential backoff with jitter for repeated 429s
Reset internal counters when X-RateLimit-Reset passes

data.title: Python client respecting rate limits
data.content: Client-side rate limit tracking using response headers.

data.title: Rate limit headers on every response
data.text: Send rate limit headers on every response, not just 429. Clients need to see their remaining quota before they hit the limit. Sending headers only on errors is an anti-pattern.

items.question: Should X-RateLimit-Reset be a Unix timestamp or seconds?
items.answer: Document it clearly. Unix timestamps are unambiguous. Seconds-until-reset is easier for clients but ambiguous across time zones. The RFC 6585 draft recommends seconds.

items.question: What if the client ignores the headers?
items.answer: You cannot force clients to respect headers. Return 429 with Retry-After when they exceed the limit. Log clients that ignore headers for monitoring and potential blocking.

items.question: Should I include rate limits in the OpenAPI spec?
items.answer: Yes. Use the x-* extension fields to document rate limit behavior. This lets SDK generators include rate limit awareness in client libraries.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Send rate limit headers on every response, not just errors.
Support both de facto and RFC 6585 header names.
Document your header semantics in the OpenAPI spec.
data.takeaway: Rate limit headers are the API's way of telling clients how to behave. Send them on every request, and clients will self-regulate instead of hammering your 429 endpoint.
